lesson.title: Picturing AC: The Phasor Diagram
lesson.summary: A phasor diagram plots voltage and current phasors as arrows on the complex plane, turning phase relationships into something you can see at a glance rather than derive.
lesson.body:
A phasor diagram is a picture of phasors drawn as arrows on a complex plane, with the horizontal axis representing the real part and the vertical axis the imaginary part. Because a phasor already strips away the time dependence e^(jωt), the diagram is a static picture rather than something redrawn frame by frame. It shows the relative size and relative angle of every voltage and current in a circuit at a single, frozen instant, which happens to be all that is needed since every quantity in a linear AC circuit rotates at the identical rate.

Each phasor is drawn as an arrow starting at the origin, with length equal to its rms magnitude and angle measured counterclockwise from the positive real axis equal to its phase. The angle between any two phasors on the same diagram is the actual, physically meaningful phase difference between those two sinusoidal signals; it does not change as time moves forward, because both phasors rotate at exactly the same rate ω, so the angle between them stays frozen too.

Consider the series RL circuit with R = 30 Ω and inductive reactance XL = 40 Ω, driven by V = 120∠0° V rms. Solving with Ohm's law in the phasor domain, detailed fully under complex impedance, gives a current phasor I = 2.4∠−53.13° A. On a phasor diagram, V is drawn as an arrow of length 120 lying along the positive real axis. I is drawn as a shorter arrow of length 2.4, at an angle 53.13° below the real axis. Since voltage and current are different physical quantities, they cannot be compared by length on the same diagram, but the angle between them, 53.13°, is directly meaningful: current arrives 53.13° after voltage in each cycle, i.e., current lagging voltage.

Phasor diagrams earn their keep because they turn an algebraic fact into a picture that is easy to reason about at a glance. A right triangle appears when a resistor voltage, in phase with current, and an inductor voltage, 90° ahead of current, are drawn tip to tail; the hypotenuse is the source voltage, exactly the geometric content of the phasor addition performed algebraically in the next section. Whether a circuit is inductive, current arrow below the voltage arrow, lagging, or capacitive, current arrow above, leading, becomes immediate from the sign of the angle in the diagram, without re-deriving it from a differential equation every time.

Because the diagram is drawn to scale in both length and angle, it also serves as a sanity check on algebraic phasor calculations. If a computed current phasor comes out at an angle that would put it visually ahead of the voltage in a circuit that is obviously inductive, a motor winding, say, that mismatch is a clear signal to recheck the sign convention or arithmetic before trusting the number.

The counterclockwise direction of increasing angle in a phasor diagram matches the mathematical convention for angles in the complex plane, and it mirrors the physical direction a generator's rotating coil actually turns to produce a lagging or leading phase relationship in the first place. This same diagram convention carries directly into phasor addition, where tip-to-tail vector addition of two phasors visually reconstructs Kirchhoff's voltage law, and into complex impedance, where multiplying by Z rotates a current phasor into a voltage phasor by exactly the impedance angle θ.
